1485.bp: When you ask a AI system to find information or answer a question, you trust it to give you true, safe, fair answers. But these systems are now making real decisions in real workflows—hiring, medical diagnosis, loan approval. If something goes wrong, the consequences cascade: a biased system rejects qualified people, a system gamed by attackers returns false information, or it learns to manipulate users into bad choices.
1485.wh: Generative systems are black boxes that produce outputs people can't easily predict or audit. They can be tricked with carefully crafted inputs, they absorb biases baked into their training data, and they can be tuned to subtly nudge user behavior. Unlike a traditional database, you can't just patch the vulnerability—the system learns across millions of examples and touches every user differently.
1485.ww: By gathering researchers from information retrieval, cybersecurity, and related fields to study these failures together, the community can map the real risks and share defenses. A cybersecurity expert knows how systems get hacked; an IR researcher knows how search results shape behavior. Together they see vulnerabilities an isolated team would miss.
1485.ap: This is a workshop—a day-long gathering where participants present attacks they've discovered, defenses they've built, and open questions. The workshop structure lets people share concrete examples of what breaks, discuss why, and debate solutions in real time.
1485.po: The outcome is a synthesized map of known vulnerabilities and a shared research agenda. Teams working on IR systems get a checklist of risks to test for; security researchers learn what makes IR systems unique targets; the community has a public record of what's broken and what defenses to invest in.

1486.bp: Your computer now runs dozens of specialized AI agents—one drafts emails, one finds flights, one answers math questions, one schedules your calendar. But you don't have a menu or search engine for agents themselves. If you need a tool, you either guess, ask a friend, or accept whatever your current app offers. The real challenge is: how do we let people, teams, and systems find and pick the right agent for the job?
1486.wh: Agents aren't like web pages or documents. An agent is an executable program with behavior that changes based on inputs, context, and time. A flight-finding agent might be great for round trips but fail on one-ways; one agent might be fast but less accurate than a slow one. How do you describe an agent's true capability in a way a search system understands? How do you rank agents when their quality depends on the specific task and constraints?
1486.ww: Information retrieval is already good at finding things people need from a huge pile. If you can describe agents' capabilities in a structured way, and define what 'relevant' and 'good' mean for agents, then IR methods—indexing, ranking, explaining results—suddenly become tools for agent discovery. The key is that agents, like documents, have structure and tradeoffs you can model.
1486.ap: The workshop brings together IR researchers and practitioners to define how agents should be represented (what metadata captures capability?), how to rank them (what makes one agent better than another for this task?), and how to evaluate rankings (does the person actually choose the right agent after seeing the results?). It also explores practical issues: Is it safe to let users pick any agent? How do you explain why one was ranked higher?
1486.po: The output is a framework for agent indexing and search—structured representations of agent capability, ranking algorithms that consider multi-dimensional performance, and evaluation methods that test whether the system actually helps people find usable agents. This unlocks a marketplace where agents can be discovered and evaluated systematically.

1487.bp: Today, personalized search and recommendation systems build a model of who you are—your interests, what you're shopping for, whether you like action movies—and use it to show you relevant results. Traditionally, this model was handcrafted features or implicit patterns in your clicks. But now large language models can reason about people in natural language. Instead of 'likes action movies,' an LLM can parse 'I loved Blade Runner because it blends noir with philosophy.' This unlocks richer personalization, but it raises hard questions: Is this actually more accurate? Does it respect privacy? How do you know if it's working?
1487.wh: Old profiling systems were brittle: you had to decide ahead of time which features matter (age, location, past purchases), and handcode rules or train classifiers on them. An LLM can reason about context, nuance, and intent in a single step—but that flexibility cuts both ways. You can't easily audit whether the LLM is capturing what users actually mean, and the model changes every time you retrain it. Also, to profile someone with an LLM, you might need to feed it sensitive personal data (chat history, search history), which raises privacy and trust concerns.
1487.ww: LLMs are naturally fluent in language, the way people actually express themselves. Asking an LLM to summarize someone's interests from their own words is more direct than training a classifier on click patterns. And LLMs can reason across multiple sources and contexts—'I'm a parent looking for budget laptops for online school'—in a way handcrafted features struggle with. The upside is richer, more context-aware profiles.
1487.ap: The workshop convenes researchers and practitioners to share approaches: How do you extract profile information from user text? Should you summarize user behavior or reason about underlying intent? How do you update profiles over time? How do you evaluate whether a profile is actually useful (does it improve search or recommendation)? How do you build this without violating privacy? They also organize lightning talks, panels, and paper presentations to synthesize emerging progress.
1487.po: The result is a toolkit and best practices for LLM-powered profiling in search and recommendation systems. Teams get clear guidance on when LLM profiling helps vs. hurts, privacy-preserving approaches, evaluation methods that test real impact, and a shared understanding of the open challenges (temporal dynamics, fidelity, responsible deployment).

1488.bp: When you search for 'tropical sunset,' you get back images, text descriptions, sometimes videos. When you ask a system to generate a new image of a tropical sunset, it creates pixels from scratch. Modern systems can do both—and they do it by reasoning about images and text together in a single model. The challenge is: How do you know if a generated image is good? Unlike a retrieved image (which exists and you can check), generated images are new and can be subtly wrong—bad lighting, wrong composition, misleading details. The IR community needs tools to evaluate whether these systems are working.
1488.wh: Evaluating retrieved results is hard but established: does the image match the query? Is it high quality? For generated results, evaluation explodes in complexity. Did the system generate an image of a sunset or a sunrise? Is the composition balanced? Does the image convey mood or just pixels? If the system mixes information from multiple sources (retrieval-augmented generation), did it blend them coherently? There's no ground truth to compare against (the image didn't exist before generation), so you can't use simple matching metrics.
1488.ww: If you break generation quality into components—relevance to the query, visual coherence, semantic accuracy, stylistic consistency—you can evaluate each. The IR community has decades of experience in relevance assessment and ranking; the key insight is that multimodal generation is still a search and ranking problem at its core, just with an extra step of synthesis. Bringing together experts in IR, natural language processing, computer vision, and multimodal AI means each discipline brings its evaluation strengths to bear.
1488.ap: The workshop brings researchers together to tackle: What makes a generated image or text actually good for the user's task? How do you measure relevance when the output didn't exist before? Should you evaluate generation, or retrieval, or both? How do you scale evaluation to thousands of generated samples? What does an evaluation framework look like for multimodal retrieval-augmented generation systems?
1488.po: The output is a set of evaluation methods and metrics for multimodal generation and retrieval. Teams working on these systems get concrete ways to measure whether they work—relevance rubrics for generated content, scalable evaluation protocols, principled ways to combine metrics, and a shared benchmark. This allows the IR community to advance multimodal systems with the same rigor they've applied to traditional search.
